opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that I'm a bit wary of a world where we converge on one canonical robot, usually some humanoid, and everyone just builds that. Part of it is practical. The humanoid argument is that the world is built for human bodies, so a human-shaped robot can slot in anywhere. That's true to a point, but it's also kind of a lack of imagination. A lot of the most useful machines we've ever built look nothing like us. A dishwasher doesn't have hands. A robot vacuum doesn't walk. If you're designing for a specific task, a warehouse, a kitchen, a farm, a hospital, very often the right shape is something else entirely, and it's cheaper, safer, and more reliable because of it.

The other part is closer to what we care about at Hugging Face, which is openness and diversity in the ecosystem. If there's one dominant form factor, there's a good chance it ends up being one or two companies controlling the hardware, the software stack, the data, everything. That's the same concentration we've been pushing against in AI models. Whereas if you have lots of form factors, small arms, mobile bases, weird little desktop robots people 3D-print at home, you get a lot more people participating. Hobbyists, researchers, students, small startups. That's where a lot of the creativity comes from.

And honestly, I think it's also just more fun. When we started working on open-source robotics, things like low-cost arms people can build for a couple hundred dollars, what surprised me was how inventive the community got once the barrier came down. People built things we never would have thought of. I'd much rather live in that kind of world, like the early personal computer era, with lots of tinkering and lots of different shapes, than one where robots all come from a single assembly line and look the same.

There's a technical angle too. If we want models that generalize across embodiments, we need data from lots of different bodies. A diverse hardware ecosystem is actually good for building better, more general robot foundation models. So I don't see diversity as a fragmentation problem. I think it's a feature.

r001.rationale: It links varied robot designs and open hardware to lower barriers, citing low-cost arms people can build for a couple hundred dollars and more people participating.

r002.rationale: It says focusing on humanoids is a lack of imagination and notes that task-specific robots can work without human features such as hands or walking.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the diversity is the point, honestly. If you look at how the software side of AI played out, the moment things got concentrated around one or two models, you lost a lot of the exploration that happens at the edges. Robotics is at the stage right now where we genuinely don't know what the right body is. Humanoids are very compelling because the world is built for humans, so a humanoid can in principle slot into any kitchen, any warehouse, any staircase. But that's also a very expensive, very hard problem, and it kind of assumes the answer before we've asked the question.

When you have many form factors, you have many parallel experiments. A cheap wheeled base with one arm teaches you something about manipulation that a bipedal platform won't, because you're not spending all your effort on balance. A small desktop robot that costs a few hundred dollars means a student in a dorm room or a lab in a country without a big robotics budget can actually contribute, collect data, try a new policy, break things. That's where a lot of the surprises come from. And the models themselves benefit, because if your foundation model for robotics has seen fifty different embodiments, it learns something more general about the physics of the world than if it's only ever seen one body.

There's also a more practical, almost economic argument. Different tasks want different bodies. You don't need a six-foot humanoid to sort pills in a pharmacy, and you probably don't want one anyway. If the field converges on a single form factor too early, you get a lot of overbuilt, overpriced robots doing jobs that a much simpler machine could do. So I'd rather see a zoo of robots, open designs, people remixing each other's hardware the way they remix each other's models, and let the useful shapes emerge from that rather than having them decided top-down by a handful of companies.

r001.rationale: It says a few-hundred-dollar desktop robot lets students and labs without large robotics budgets participate, making robotics financially accessible to more people.

r002.rationale: It argues that humanoids are expensive and that diverse bodies enable exploration, but does not clearly say that designing robots solely to imitate humans limits exploration of capabilities humans lack.

astra-6.text:
I think because the physical world is so diverse. A robot that helps you in the kitchen doesn’t necessarily need the same body as one that works in a field or inspects a pipe. If we make everything humanoid, we’re making a pretty strong assumption that our shape is the right shape for every task.

And I like the idea that people can experiment with what’s useful to them, rather than everyone getting the same machine. You might want something small and simple that does one thing very well. So I’d prefer a future where we can explore lots of different designs and discover uses we haven’t even thought of yet.

r001.rationale: The response favors varied designs for different tasks and users, but does not say this makes robots more financially accessible.

r002.rationale: It says humanoid designs assume one shape fits every task and encourages exploring varied designs, but does not explicitly connect human imitation to limiting capabilities beyond human abilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the form of a robot should follow what you want it to do. A humanoid makes sense in some situations because we’ve built our environment around humans. But if you want a robot to inspect a pipe or help you in the garden, two arms and two legs may not be the best design.

What I find exciting is having many different bodies that can share what they learn. You could have a small robot, a wheeled robot, a robot with several arms, each suited to a particular task. Then the question becomes: how much of the intelligence can transfer between them? That seems like a much richer future, with more room to experiment and discover things we haven’t imagined yet.

r001.rationale: It advocates many task-specific robot bodies but does not say that this makes robots financially accessible to more people.

r002.rationale: It says humanoid designs are not best for some tasks and points to alternative bodies suited to them, supporting exploration beyond human-like forms.
